source.title: Latent Taxonomies: How Property Induction Develops in Language Model Pre-training
source.authors: Jan Sobotka; Ekaterina Goliakova; Marcin Detyniecki; Antoine Bosselut; X. Renard

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendix are present
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses published loss-scaling expectations but does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit loss-scaling laws, or test compute-optimal allocations. Its size-scaling experiments measure property induction instead.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law work as background but reports no result on held-out loss, loss-law extrapolation, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architectural effects on loss, other modalities, downstream predictability, or fit-dependence. The reported size-scaling results concern induction advantage, a different outcome; these are recorded with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. only as background for the expectation that scale helps. It measures taxonomic property induction advantage under continued pre-training with a fixed injected-data budget. It reports no held-out loss, no loss-law fits, no compute-optimal allocation and no standard downstream benchmarks. Induction advantage is a different construct from V6's downstream task performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also conclude that taxonomically aligned induction emerges from next-token prediction alone and is recoverable from entity representations. They add that it is forgotten when injection stops, interferes with learning a conflicting taxonomy, and can be overridden by in-context taxonomies.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or test the loss-scaling methods; it measures property induction in controlled continued-pretraining experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: For the induction results, model size changes the measured induction advantage under a fixed data budget. The paper also reports that increasing batch size changes absolute probabilities and the speed of induction, while preserving the qualitative ordering of memorization, within-category induction, and across-category induction.

fits_no_version.finding: With a fixed injected-data budget, induction advantage falls with model size (Pythia 70M–2.8B; OLMo 2 1B vs 7B). Larger Pythia models memorize injected facts faster.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At a fixed data budget, larger LMs memorize injected facts faster but generalize them along a latent taxonomy less strongly.

fits_no_version.finding: Induction advantage increases with the base checkpoint's prior pre-training steps (Pythia 160M 0–143k; OLMo 2 1B 0–1.9M), with a few exceptions (Figure 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More prior pre-training strengthens taxonomic property induction on newly injected facts.

record.problems: The experiments use small, balanced, noiseless taxonomies and dense synthetic-data injection. The paper notes that the fixed-data-budget scaling result varies one factor at a time, whereas practical training often scales model size and data together. Reported plotted uncertainty is across three random seeds; the paper does not report numerical uncertainty values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version result rows were available. Other results in Sections 3.1–3.5 and Appendix D concern taxonomy acquisition, representations, forgetting, interference, or in-context induction rather than the loss-scaling claim.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation of loss from small to large runs.
No shape-versus-loss comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit in other modalities or regimes. Continued pre-training is used but loss scaling is not measured.
No standard downstream task evaluation versus scale or loss. Induction advantage on injected synthetic facts is a different construct.
No comparison of fits or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The relation was changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': scaling-law work appears only as a one-sentence motivation in Section 3.3 and in the Limitations' note that size and data are usually scaled together. The fixed-data-budget size effect is not evidence against V3, because no compute-optimal allocation is tested. The checkpoint-maturity result (Figure 4) has no row; it is listed under fits_no_version, not missing, since it bears on no version.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction of larger-run loss from fits on smaller runs.
No compute-budget sweep or measurement of loss-minimising parameter and token counts.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count using loss.
No loss-scaling test in other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task performance evaluation or relation between downstream performance and pretraining loss.
No comparison of loss-law fits or compute-optimal allocations under different fitting choices or setups.

rows.subject: Pythia family
rows.operation_detail: Compared induction advantage across model sizes using identical injected data and a fixed data budget; reported values average the last 1,000 injection steps.
rows.value: The induction advantage decreases with model size; the 70M Pythia model shows the strongest correct induction, while larger models show relatively weak induction, most clearly at the endpoints.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the mean across three random seeds is shown in Figure 5; numerical uncertainty values not stated.
rows.note: This is a result about taxonomic property induction, not held-out loss or a loss-scaling law.
rows.check: Induction advantage under a fixed injected-data budget is not a loss or downstream-task measure for any version. The reader's 'observed' only means the size trend was seen, so it is not a claim-version state. The baseline is effectively zero advantage (within = across) and is not stated.

rows.subject: OLMo 2 family
rows.operation_detail: Compared induction advantage across model sizes using identical injected data and a fixed data budget; reported values average the last 1,000 injection steps.
rows.value: The induction advantage decreases with model size; OLMo 2 1B shows the strongest correct induction, while larger models show relatively weak induction, most clearly at the endpoints.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the mean across three random seeds is shown in Figure 5; numerical uncertainty values not stated.
rows.note: This is a result about taxonomic property induction, not held-out loss or a loss-scaling law.
rows.check: Same as R1: the measure is not linked to any version. Only two sizes (1B, 7B) are compared, so 'decreases with model size' rests on two points.

rows.subject: Pythia family
rows.operation_detail: Compared memorization speed and early induction advantage across model sizes; induction advantage is averaged over the first 1,000 continued-pretraining steps.
rows.value: Larger models memorize faster, while the downward trend in induction advantage shows that they generalize along the taxonomy more slowly.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the mean across three random seeds is shown in Figure 12; numerical uncertainty values not stated.
rows.note: The measures concern memorization and property induction, not held-out loss.
rows.check: Memorization speed and early induction advantage are not a loss-scaling or downstream measure. Two measures are combined in one row; they could be split.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
